title: ensureVecTable drops the vector table (destroying all embeddings) on any dimension change
Vector dimension check uses substring includes(), so float[38] matches float[384]
body:
## Description

`ensureVecTable()` decides whether the existing `memory_vec` table has the right dimension by doing a substring `includes()` check against the table's stored DDL:

```ts
const expected = `float[${dim}]`;
if (!row || !row.sql.includes(expected)) {
  // Drop and recreate with the correct dimension
  ...
}
```

(`packages/infrastructure/src/database/sqlite.adapter.ts:101-102`).

Because `String.prototype.includes` matches any substring, `expected = "float[38]"` is considered present in a table whose DDL contains `embedding float[384]` (the text `float[384]` contains `float[38]`). The check therefore passes for a *different*, wrong dimension. The same prefix-collision happens for any dimension that is a textual prefix of another (e.g. 12 vs 128, 76 vs 768).

## Impact

A 38-dimensional embedding will be accepted against a 384-dimensional table (and similar prefix collisions). sqlite-vec then either rejects the malformed insert at runtime or, worse, silently stores/compares vectors of the wrong shape, corrupting similarity results. The faulty comparison also undermines the dimension-mismatch logic that is supposed to protect the table, producing inconsistent behaviour depending on the exact numbers involved. This is a correctness bug affecting all vector storage and search paths.

## Required Fix

1. Parse the actual dimension out of the stored DDL (e.g. with a regex like `/float\[(\d+)\]/`) and compare it numerically to `dim`, instead of doing a substring search.
2. Add unit tests covering prefix-colliding dimensions such as `(38, 384)` and `(12, 128)` to lock in the correct behaviour.

## References

- CWE-697: Incorrect Comparison (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/697.html)

title: Memory store/update write three tables without a transaction, drifting the vector index out of sync
body:
## Description

`SQLiteMemoryRepository.store()` and `update()` each mutate three separate tables — `memory_entries`, the `memory_entries_fts` full-text index, and the `memory_vec` vector index — using independent `prepare().run()` calls with no surrounding transaction:

```ts
const row = insert.get(...) as { rowid: number };

// Update FTS index
this.db
  .prepare(`INSERT INTO memory_entries_fts(rowid, content, tags) VALUES (?, ?, ?)`)
  .run(row.rowid, entry.content, JSON.stringify(entry.tags ?? []));

// Store embedding if provided
if (entry.embedding && entry.embedding.length > 0) {
  this.ensureVecTable(entry.embedding.length);
  this.db
    .prepare(`INSERT INTO memory_vec(rowid, embedding) VALUES (?, ?)`)
    .run(BigInt(row.rowid), serializeEmbedding(entry.embedding));
}
```

(`packages/infrastructure/src/database/sqlite.adapter.ts:111-143`; the same non-atomic pattern appears in `update()` at `sqlite.adapter.ts:190-230`, which deletes/re-inserts the FTS and vec rows separately).

If any statement after the first throws (e.g. `ensureVecTable` recreates the table, a serialization error, a constraint violation, or a crash between calls), the writes that already succeeded are committed while the rest are not.

## Impact

Partial writes leave the three stores inconsistent: a base row with no FTS entry (invisible to keyword search) or no vector (invisible to semantic search), or a vector/FTS row pointing at a base row that was never inserted. Once drifted, queries silently return incomplete or stale results and the divergence is permanent because nothing reconciles the indexes. For an update, a thrown `ensureVecTable` after the base-row `UPDATE` commits the new content but leaves the old embedding in place. This is a data-integrity defect across the memory subsystem.

## Required Fix

1. Wrap the multi-table mutations in `store()` and `update()` in a single transaction using better-sqlite3's `db.transaction(fn)`, so all three tables commit or roll back together.
2. Move `ensureVecTable()` schema changes out of the per-row write path (DDL inside a transaction is itself problematic) so the transactional inserts operate on a stable schema.
3. Apply the same transactional wrapping to `delete()` and `compact()` (`sqlite.adapter.ts:235-260`), which also touch all three tables sequentially.

## References

- CWE-662: Improper Synchronization (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/662.html)
- SQLite transactions: https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html

title: Each repository opens its own better-sqlite3 connection to the same database file
Agent loop timeout throws inside a setTimeout callback (uncaught crash) and never aborts in-flight work
processMessage mutates the caller's messages array in place
body:
## Description

`AgentRuntime.processMessage()` builds the agent context by assigning the caller-supplied `messages` array **by reference** to `conversationHistory`:

```ts
async processMessage(messages: Message[], agent: IAgent): Promise<string> {
  const context: AgentContext = {
    sessionId: crypto.randomUUID(),
    userId: "direct",
    conversationHistory: messages,
    ...
  };
  const result = await this.runAgenticLoop(agent, context);
  ...
}
```

(`packages/core/src/usecases/agent-runtime.ts:116-128`).

`runAgenticLoop` then appends tool-result turns directly onto that same array:

```ts
context.conversationHistory.push({
  role: "tool",
  content: JSON.stringify(actionResult.output),
  timestamp: new Date(),
  metadata: { toolName: action.toolName },
});
```

(`packages/core/src/usecases/agent-runtime.ts:180-185`). Because `conversationHistory` is the *same* object the caller passed in, every pushed turn mutates the caller's array.

## Impact

The caller's `messages` array is silently extended with internal tool turns after each `processMessage` call. Callers that reuse or inspect that array (e.g. maintaining their own conversation buffer and calling `processMessage` repeatedly) accumulate duplicate/foreign turns, leading to ballooning context, replayed tool outputs, and surprising state shared across calls. This is a side-effect bug that violates the principle of least astonishment for a method that looks read-only with respect to its input.

## Required Fix

1. Copy the incoming messages into a new array before assigning to `conversationHistory`, e.g. `conversationHistory: [...messages]`.
2. Optionally document that `processMessage` does not mutate its arguments, and add a regression test asserting the input array length is unchanged after the call.

## References

- CWE-1325: Improperly Controlled Sequential Memory Allocation (related, via unbounded array growth) (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1325.html)
- General guidance: treat function arguments as immutable; copy before mutating.

title: getRegisteredTools returns empty parameters, discarding real tool schemas
body:
## Description

`AgentRuntime.getRegisteredTools()` builds the `ToolDefinition[]` advertised to the agent/LLM, but hardcodes an empty parameter schema and a placeholder description:

```ts
getRegisteredTools(): ToolDefinition[] {
  return Array.from(this.toolRegistry.entries()).map(([name, _executor]) => ({
    name,
    description: `Tool: ${name}`,
    parameters: {},
    scope: "default",
  }));
}
```

(`packages/core/src/usecases/agent-runtime.ts:51-58`). `ToolDefinition` is declared with a real `parameters: Record<string, unknown>` field (`packages/core/src/domain/agent.interface.ts:46-51`), but the registry's `ToolExecutor` type only carries `name` and `execute()` (`agent-runtime.ts:27-30`), so there is nowhere for a schema to come from — every tool is exposed with `parameters: {}` and a generated description.

## Impact

The LLM is told each tool takes no/unknown arguments and is given no meaningful description, so it cannot reliably produce correct `toolArgs`. Tool calls degrade to guesswork: the model may omit required arguments or invent parameter names, causing tool executions to fail or behave incorrectly. The advertised tool contract does not match what the executors actually expect. This undermines the core think-act-observe loop and is a correctness defect.

## Required Fix

1. Extend `ToolExecutor` (and `registerTool`) to carry a real `description` and a `parameters` JSON schema for each tool.
2. Have `getRegisteredTools()` surface those real values instead of `parameters: {}` / `Tool: ${name}`.
3. Validate `toolArgs` against the declared schema in `executeAction` before invoking the executor.

## References

- CWE-573: Improper Following of Specification by Caller (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/573.html)

title: SQLite connections set no busy_timeout and are never closed on shutdown
searchByEmbedding selects the vector distance but discards it, exposing no relevance score
body:
## Description

`searchByEmbedding()` runs a KNN query that selects and orders by the sqlite-vec `distance`, but the value is then thrown away by the row mapper:

```ts
const rows = this.db
  .prepare(`
    SELECT me.*, v.distance
    FROM memory_vec v
    JOIN memory_entries me ON me.rowid = v.rowid
    WHERE v.embedding MATCH ? AND v.k = ?
    ORDER BY v.distance
  `)
  .all(serializeEmbedding(embedding), limit) as Record<string, unknown>[];

return rows.map((r) => this.rowToEntry(r));
```

(`packages/infrastructure/src/database/sqlite.adapter.ts:170-188`). `rowToEntry` (`sqlite.adapter.ts:262-271`) maps only the base `memory_entries` columns and never reads `r.distance`, so the selected distance is dropped on the floor.

Note: rows are still returned in ascending-distance order via the SQL `ORDER BY v.distance`, so the ordering itself is correct; the defect is that the numeric similarity score is not surfaced to callers.

## Impact

Callers receive an ordered list of `MemoryEntry` objects but have no access to the per-result distance/similarity score, so they cannot apply a relevance threshold (e.g. drop results above a distance cutoff), display confidence, or blend semantic ranking with other signals. The query pays to compute and sort by distance, then discards it, forcing any downstream relevance logic to either re-compute distances or treat all returned memories as equally relevant. This is a low-severity correctness/usability gap in the memory retrieval API.

## Required Fix

1. Surface the distance/score to callers — e.g. extend the return type (or add a sibling method) to include `{ entry, distance }`, or thread the score onto a `MemoryEntry` metadata field.
2. Optionally use the exposed score to support a relevance threshold parameter on `searchByEmbedding`.

## References

- sqlite-vec KNN / distance: https://github.com/asg017/sqlite-vec

title: EnvSecretsAdapter.delete cannot remove env-provided secrets and set is non-persistent
registerAdapter types the implementation as any, bypassing the DI cradle type check
body:
## Description

The DI helper that registers infrastructure adapters constrains the registration *name* to a key of the cradle, but types the implementation as `any`:

```ts
export function registerAdapter<K extends keyof CradleInterface>(
  container: AppContainer,
  name: K,

  implementation: any
): void {
  container.register(name, asClass(implementation).singleton());
}
```

(`packages/core/src/ports/di.container.ts:93-100`).

Because `implementation` is `any`, TypeScript performs no check that the class being registered under `name` actually produces a `CradleInterface[K]`. Any class (or even a non-class value) can be registered under, say, `"memoryRepository"` and the compiler stays silent.

## Impact

The cradle's strong typing is defeated at exactly the boundary where wiring mistakes happen. Registering an adapter that does not implement the expected port — or registering it under the wrong key — compiles cleanly and only fails at runtime (or silently misbehaves) when the dependency is resolved. This removes a compile-time safety net for the IoC container and is a type-safety regression, albeit low severity since it affects developer-time guarantees rather than runtime behaviour directly.

## Required Fix

1. Type the implementation as a constructor that yields the matching cradle member, e.g. `implementation: new (...args: any[]) => CradleInterface[K]` (or a `Constructor<CradleInterface[K]>` helper type), so mismatches are caught at compile time.
2. Remove the `any` and the stray blank line, and verify existing `registerAdapter` call sites still type-check against the tightened signature.

## References

- CWE-758: Reliance on Undefined, Unspecified, or Implementation-Defined Behavior (related) (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/758.html)
- TypeScript guidance on avoiding `any` at API boundaries: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#any

title: AgentOrchestrator.processPendingTasks re-creates duplicate tasks and never executes the pending ones
InMemoryEventBus uses a redundant allSettled pattern
rejectionReason: Verified safe — not a defect. In publish() (packages/infrastructure/src/events/in-memory-event-bus.ts:12-23) each handler invocation is individually wrapped in `.catch()` that logs and swallows the error, so every element of the `promises` array always resolves; `Promise.allSettled(promises)` then awaits all of them. Handler isolation is therefore already correct: a throwing/rejecting handler logs its error and does NOT prevent the other handlers from running or cause publish() to reject, and publish() still awaits completion of every handler. The only observation is that `allSettled` is interchangeable with `Promise.all` here (since the per-handler `.catch()` already guarantees no rejection) — a harmless stylistic redundancy, not a reliability bug. No code change is warranted.
